title: Website Review — Tuğba Bozçağa (https://tugbabozcaga.github.io/)
text:
Prepared in advance of the Oxford CASSM/DPIR–DSPI Associate Professorship shortlist meeting. Covers all six pages (About, Research, Teaching, Geospatial Analysis in R, Other, Vita).
This version replaces the v1 review. Two factual claims in v1 have been corrected: (i) the Springer chapter _12 URL is the correct chapter for “Syrian Refugee Integration in Turkey,” verified against Springer; the v1 claim that _25 was correct was wrong. (ii) Development Analytics is dual-located — UK Companies House registers the company at 9 Marlborough Court, Oxford OX2 0QT, and the institute also lists an Istanbul address. Calling “Oxford-based” a flat factual error was wrong; the issue is that the description undersells DSPI-relevant substance, not that the geography is misstated.
The full website-vs-application inconsistency inventory (54 items) and the per-link verification table (~95 instances) are retained as Appendix A and Appendix B at the end of this document — useful for whoever does implementation but not the lead deliverable.



The site is competent and content-rich, and lands reasonably on substance — the AJPS placement, prize density, and methodological seriousness all show. But the moment a reader starts checking, three things go wrong at once.
Link integrity is broken in visible places. The flagship AJPS paper “Paper” link goes to a different paper (the Mozambique paper), and the Mozambique paper link goes to the AJPS paper — the two SSRN IDs are swapped. Eight separate links route to empty Wix template pages. Three MPSA award links return 404. Two co-author links (Harding, Kutlu) are broken. The Google Scholar link in every page header is still user=YOUR_ID. Imams and Patrons is listed as “forthcoming” but has been published in JCR since September 2025.
The site is a stale subset of the application document. The 2024 Oxford DPIR Visiting Scholar position, four-doctoral-student supervision, KCL Performance Recognition Award, MZES Mannheim 2026 workshop, Oxford DPIR/DSPI/MEC seminar talks, AALIMS Faculty Fellow status, APSA PE Council Member role, and KCL institutional service are all on the application CV and absent from the website. Several places where the website contradicts the application: AALIMS Faculty Fellow vs. site’s “Junior Fellow”; APSA Council Member vs. site’s generic “member”; three Mozambique co-authors in the application vs. two on the site.
Framing under-sells DSPI. The site reads as “political economy of development.” The application Research Statement reframes it as “political economy of development with an emphasis on service provision and social welfare” — exactly the DSPI register — and reorders the pillars. None of that has been ported.
Single most important fix: unswap the two SSRN links, replace the eight Wix stubs, fix the Scholar placeholder, and reconcile AALIMS / APSA PE / Visiting Scholar / supervision against the application CV. Then port the Research-Statement opening to the About page so the site reads DSPI-legible at first skim.







Research — “The Social Bureaucrat” and Mozambique paper SSRN links are swapped Current: The “Paper” link under “The Social Bureaucrat” (AJPS, forthcoming) resolves to abstract_id=5932234 — the Mozambique paper. The “Paper” link under “Putting Property Rights in Context” (Mozambique) resolves to abstract_id=5397681 — “The Social Bureaucrat.” Why it matters: The flagship AJPS publication and the most DSPI-legible working paper both open onto each other. A committee member opening either to read it lands on something else. Single most damaging error on the site. Suggested change: Swap the two SSRN IDs back. After the swap, open both links to confirm they resolve to the right papers before publishing.


Research — eight links route to empty Wix template pages Current: Links to tugbabozcaga.com/awardcitation1, forbearancedilution (used twice — once on the Springer chapter, once on the Holland/SCID paper), education-localcouncils, gender-meritocracy, education-dilemma, plus the Teaching page syllabus links syllabus-7aaom041 and syllabus7aaom230. All resolve to the same Wix template — header reading “Tuğba Bozçağa / Assistant Professor in Politics & Political Methodology, King’s College London / tugba.bozcaga@kcl.ac.uk” — with no paper, appendix, citation, or syllabus underneath. Worse, the Wix template still describes her as “Assistant Professor” with a stale bozcaga@mit.edu contact, contradicting the main site. Why it matters: These links promise specific content (drafts, appendices, the citation for an APSA award, KCL syllabi) and deliver nothing. To a careful reader this looks worse than a 404 — it suggests the site is built on dead stubs. The application CV also links to two of these stubs (education-localcouncils, education-dilemma), so a committee member clicking from the application document lands on the same empty pages. Suggested change: Replace each with a working link (direct PDF, SSRN, Dataverse, institutional URL) or remove until the underlying file exists. Coordinate the same fix in the application CV.


All pages — Google Scholar link is a placeholder Current: https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=YOUR_ID in the header of all six pages. Why it matters: Most visible “unfinished site” signal on the entire site. The real profile exists. Suggested change: Replace with https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=rkJvZccAAAAJ&hl=en.


Research — “Imams and Patrons” listed as “Forthcoming” but published in JCR (Sept 2025) Current (both website and application): “Forthcoming in Journal of Conflict Resolution”; “Paper” link → SSRN abstract_id=5397663. Why it matters: The paper has been published online in JCR since September 2025 (DOI 10.1177/00220027251374830). Listing it as forthcoming understates the record. The SSRN page at 5397663 returns 403 to outside fetches; v1 was wrong to claim the ID is invalid, but the right move regardless is to point readers at the published version, not SSRN. Suggested change: Update both website and application CV to: “‘Imams and Patrons: Service Provision by Islamist Non-State Actors’ (with Fotini Christia). Journal of Conflict Resolution, 2025.” Replace the SSRN link with the published Sage URL: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00220027251374830.


Research — Mozambique paper missing fourth co-author (Pita Barros) Current: Listed on the website as “with Robin Harding and Arinze Nwokolo.” Why it matters: The application Research Statement lists “Robin Harding (Oxford), Arinze Nwokolo (Lagos Business School), and Henrique Pita Barros (ISEG Lisbon).” The website is missing one co-author of a paper described as “about to be submitted to APSR.” Authorship omissions are taken seriously. Suggested change: Add Pita Barros to the website entry. Match the application’s authorship list exactly.


Research — three MPSA award links and three more dead/broken links Current (About page): mpsanet.org/professional-resources/awards/2022-award-recipients/ is used three times for Pi Sigma Alpha, Kenneth Meier, and Best Paper by an Emerging Scholar — all 404. Research page: Robin Harding linked as robingharding.org (extra “g,” broken); Rabia Kutlu linked as rabiakutlu.com (dead domain, used twice); Turkish Policy Quarterly paper links to turkishpolicy.com (now a “domain for sale” page). Why it matters: Three broken links in the most-read paragraph of the About page; broken co-author links to two scholars (Harding is at Oxford DPIR — the appointing department); her earliest publication unreachable. The application CV uses correct URLs for Harding and Kutlu’s Stanford page; only the website has the broken versions. Suggested change: Update MPSA links to mpsanet.org/professional-resources/awards/award-recipient-archive/. Fix Harding to https://robinharding.org/ and Kutlu to https://politicalscience.stanford.edu/people/rabia-kutlu-karasu. For TPQ, find an archived copy (Wayback, ResearchGate) or remove the link and keep the citation.


Other — five MIT/first-gen links dead or 404; APSA committee URL inconsistent with About page Current: (a) oge.mit.edu/finances/graduate-student-life-grants/ → 404; (b) firstgen.mit.edu/ and (c) firstgen.mit.edu/resources → dead domain (MIT FGP moved to advising.mit.edu/fli/); (d) oge.mit.edu/community-diversity/dei-committee/ → 404; (e) APSA First-Gen Committee URL (/RESOURCES/For-Faculty/...) errors out, while the About page uses a different working URL. Why it matters: Five out of nine substantive links on a page that anchors her first-gen organising work are broken; the same APSA committee gets two different (one broken, one working) URLs across the site. Suggested change: Replace MIT FGP links with https://advising.mit.edu/fli/; remove or replace the dead OGE links; use the working APSA committee URL from the About page consistently.


About — research framing diverges from application Research Statement Current (website): “My research focuses on the political economy of development, particularly public service provision and social welfare.” Why it matters: The application opens with stronger DSPI-legible framing — “political economy of development, with an emphasis on service provision and social welfare” — gives a different pillar order, and identifies colonial extraction and disaster resilience as her forward research agenda. None of this strategic framing is on the website. A committee reading both will read the website as a stale, pre-strategic version of the candidate. Suggested change: Port the application Research Statement opening directly to the About page. Match the application’s pillar order: (1) state capacity / service delivery; (2) colonial extraction; (3) refugee mobility & climate vulnerability; (4) disaster resilience.


About — methods sentence undersells for a CASSM-targeted post Current (website): “I study these issues … through quasi-experimental statistical designs and novel data sources, often supplemented by fieldwork and archival research.” Why it matters: The post is “Causal and Experimental Methods in Politics and Social Policy.” The application names methods specifically; the website doesn’t. Suggested change (adapted, not ported verbatim): “Methodologically, I use causal and quasi-experimental designs — including spatial regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences, event-study, panel, and spatial econometric approaches — combined with fieldwork, archival research, and novel data sources such as satellite imagery, administrative data, and mobile-phone records.”


Research — Oxford DPIR Visiting Scholar (2024) entirely missing Current (application CV): “2024 University of Oxford. Visiting Scholar, Department of Politics and IR.” Why it matters: Of all positions on the CV, this one is the strongest possible signal for this specific committee — she has held a visiting position in the appointing department. Invisible on the website. Suggested change: Add to About page. Combine with Nuffield, phrased as past since the application CV gives 2024 with no end-date marker: “In 2024, I was a Visiting Scholar at Oxford’s Department of Politics and International Relations, and I am an Associate Member of Nuffield College, Oxford.”


Research — five working papers and two in-progress projects are title-only Current (website): “Employment Type and Refugees’ Climate Vulnerability…”, “Regulatory Failures in Disaster-Prone Times…”, “Scarcity and Discrimination in Local Public Services…”, “Urban Bias in Rural Governance…” — titles only. No links, abstracts, or one-line descriptions. Why it matters: These are the most DSPI-legible projects on the entire site. Title-only listings make them invisible. The application has detailed paragraphs on the climate vulnerability paper (CORINE land cover, mobile CDRs, temperature/precipitation) and the wildfire paper (privatisation, electoral records, NASA Global Fire Atlas, difference-in-differences). The application also reveals: “When Incumbent Mayors…” is “About to be submitted to American Journal of Political Science” and the Mozambique paper is “About to be submitted to American Political Science Review” — submission status absent from website. Suggested change: Port one-or-two-sentence descriptions from the Research Statement. Add submission status where the application provides it.


Vita — page is essentially empty AND the linked CV PDF is older than the application CV Current: The Vita page contains only a download link. The website’s cv.pdf is “Last updated August 2025.” The application CV is “Last updated April 2026.” Why it matters: Two different CV documents are circulating. A reader following the website link gets an older version than the one accompanying the application — and the August 2025 version contains “Phi Bheta Kappa Award” (typo), “Imams and Businessmen” (outdated paper title), and the now-stale “forthcoming” status for Imams and Patrons. References will likely receive the April 2026 version; the committee, comparing, will see drift. Suggested change: (a) Replace cv.pdf with the corrected April 2026 application CV (after fixing Pi Sigma Alpha and the propagated URL errors); (b) add a short HTML version of key CV sections (Education, Positions, Selected Awards, Recent Talks, Service) to the Vita page; (c) include a “Last updated” date.


Application document — MPSA award name appears five different ways across her own materials Current: Application Research Statement: “MPSA Phi Beta Kappa Award.” Application CV Publications section: “Phi Beta Kappa Award, MPSA.” Application CV Awards section: “MPSA Phi Sigma Alpha Award.” Website About: “Pi Sigma Alpha Award” (correct). Website CV PDF: “Phi Bheta Kappa Award” (typo of the wrong honor society). Why it matters: The correct MPSA prize is Pi Sigma Alpha. “Phi Beta Kappa” is a different, unrelated honor society — the application document has named the wrong organisation in two of three places. Anyone on the committee who knows MPSA will catch this. Five versions of the same award name across the candidate’s documents is not survivable. Suggested change: Standardise on “MPSA Pi Sigma Alpha Award (Best Paper Presented at the Annual Conference)” across application Research Statement, both CV sections, website About page, and website CV PDF.


Teaching — doctoral and dissertation supervision claim missing entirely from website Current: No mention of doctoral supervision on the website Teaching page. Why it matters: The application Teaching Statement says she supervises ~12 BA/MA dissertations per year and co-supervises four doctoral students. For a permanent post that involves doctoral training, evidence of supervision capacity should be findable. Suggested change (softer than the bureaucratic application phrasing): Add to the Teaching page: “I supervise undergraduate, master’s, and doctoral research projects in comparative political economy, political methodology, public service delivery, migration, and social welfare.” (The exact “all four passed upgrades without extension” detail belongs in the Teaching Statement, not the public site.)


About / Research — AALIMS title and APSA PE role contradict the application CV Current (website): “Junior Fellow at AALIMS”; “member of APSA’s Political Economy Section Committee.” Why it matters: The application CV (April 2026, Tuğba’s own canonical document) says “Faculty Fellow, AALIMS, 2021–” and “Council Member of the APSA Political Economy Section, 2024–.” Faculty Fellow is more senior than Junior Fellow at AALIMS, and Council Member is a more specific role than generic Section Committee member. The website is downgrading her own current titles. Suggested change: Update the website to match the application: “Faculty Fellow at AALIMS”; “Council Member of the APSA Political Economy Section.” No further verification needed — the application CV is the source.


Research — wildfire paper has three different titles across application, website, and website CV PDF Current: Application Research Statement and CV: “Privatization without Regulation: The Political Economy of Electricity Infrastructure and Wildfires.” Website Research page: “Regulatory Failures in Disaster-Prone Times: How Electricity Privatization Shapes Wildfire Outcomes.” Website CV PDF: “Regulatory Failures in Disaster-Prone Areas…”. Why it matters: Three titles for the same paper across documents the committee will read together. Inconsistency reads as carelessness even if it reflects an honest revision history. Suggested change: Standardise on the application’s “Privatization without Regulation…” version (cleanest, most CASSM-legible) across all three documents.





Research — Recent Talks section absent from website; Oxford DPIR and DSPI talks invisible Current: No talks/presentations section. Why it matters: The application CV lists 2025 talks at Oxford DPIR Comparative Politics Seminar Series and 2022 talks at Oxford DSPI Seminar Series and Oxford DPIR Seminar Series — i.e. talks to both halves of the appointing committee. “She’s already presented in our department” is one of the strongest possible signals; currently invisible to anyone without the CV PDF open. Suggested change: Add a “Recent Talks” subsection at the bottom of Research (or on Vita), listing 2024–2026 talks with the Oxford ones leading. Port the entire “Recent Talks & Presentations” section from the application CV.


About — bio omits 2024 KCL Performance Recognition Award Current: No mention; prize list ends with 2022 MPSA awards. Why it matters: The application CV’s most recent award is 2024. The website makes the recognition trail look three years old. Suggested change: Add to the About prize list, leading because most recent.


About — current research and forward-looking signal absent Current: Bio ends on dissertation/early-postdoc-era prizes. Why it matters: Reads backwards-looking. The application identifies a forward agenda (colonial extraction, disaster resilience), submitted-to-AJPS and submitted-to-APSR papers, MZES workshop, and 2024 KCL recognition. Suggested change: Add 1–2 forward-looking sentences. Whether to name the ERC/UKRI/Wellcome grant pipeline publicly is Tuğba’s call — naming specific funders before submission is more aggressive than many candidates do publicly. A safer version: “My current research extends this work into the long-run consequences of colonial extraction and the political economy of regulation, infrastructure, and disaster resilience.” (If she wants the funder names public, append: “…and forms the basis of grant applications I am currently preparing.”)


About — Nuffield title and KCL title need verification and standardisation Current: Website says “Associate Faculty Member at Nuffield.” Application CV says “Associate Member, Nuffield College.” Research/Teaching Statement headers say “Lecturer in Politics (Political Methodology)”; website + application CV say “Lecturer in Politics & Political Methodology”; KCL’s main faculty page may use yet another version. Why it matters: The committee will read statements + website + CV together. Two title formats for the same role look inattentive. Suggested change: Verify Nuffield’s actual designation — “Associate Member” is the application’s version and is a real Nuffield category. For KCL, verify against the KCL faculty page and standardise across all four documents.


Other — Development Analytics description undersells DSPI relevance Current: “Development Analytics is an Oxford-based research institute that conducts evidence-based research on social programs and policy development.” Why it matters: Development Analytics is dual-located (UK Companies House registers it at 9 Marlborough Court, Oxford OX2 0QT; the institute’s contact page also lists Istanbul). Geography isn’t the issue — but the substantive areas (poverty, education, health, social protection, distributional impact of social policies) are highly DSPI-relevant and the description currently doesn’t surface them. Suggested change: “Development Analytics is a research centre and advisory working on poverty, education, health, social protection, humanitarian aid, and the distributional impact of social policies. I am a Research Associate.”


Teaching — page jumps from header to module list with no framing; no eval scores or enrolment-expansion fact Current: No teaching paragraph; modules listed as codes only; three modules have a stray ::: Quarto artefact (“PE of Development in Muslim Societies:::”, etc.). Why it matters: For a half-DSPI post, a 3–4 sentence intro signalling teaching range matters. The application Teaching Statement notes that Quantitative Research Methods received “some of the highest student assessment scores,” led to enrolment expansion, and seeded a similar undergraduate module. The website CV PDF lists evaluations of 4.7/5 (Quant Methods), 4.4/5 (PE of Development in Muslim Societies), 4.2/5 (Comparative Politics) — none on the public Teaching page. Suggested change: Fix the ::: artefacts. Add a brief intro paragraph: “My teaching spans quantitative methods, research design, comparative politics, and the political economy of development, with an emphasis on helping students apply rigorous empirical tools to questions of governance, inequality, public service delivery, migration, and social welfare.” Add level/audience and a 1-sentence content gloss per module. Surface the enrolment-expansion fact for Quant Methods.


Teaching — MZES Mannheim 2026 workshop and KCL Methods Centre roundtables absent Current: Neither mentioned. Why it matters: The application says she will deliver the Advanced Geospatial Analysis workshop at the MZES Summer School for Women in Political Methodology (May 2026) — a forward-looking, prestigious methods signal during the appointment process. Also chaired KCL Social Sciences Methods Centre PhD roundtables. Suggested change: Add both to the Teaching page (or the proposed HTML Vita) once dates and roles are confirmed.


Research — Springer chapter title and online-appendix link need correction (but the URL _12 is correct) Current: The entry is titled “Assessing Syrian Refugee Integration Using Call Detail Records from Turkey.” The Springer link link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-12554-7_12 opens the right chapter (verified). The “Online Appendix” link points to the unrelated forbearancedilution Wix stub. Why it matters: The published Springer title is “Syrian Refugee Integration in Turkey: Evidence from Call Detail Records.” The website and application CV both still use the working-paper title. The appendix link promises supplementary material but lands on an empty page. Suggested change: Update the title in both website and application CV to the published version. Keep the Springer _12 link as-is — it works. Remove or replace the “Online Appendix” link.


Research — OUP chapter title differs from published; application CV uses the wrong URL Current: Both documents use “Combining Mobile Data and Satellite Imaging for Human Mobility.” The OUP-published title is “Combining Mobile Call Data and Satellite Imaging for Human Mobility.” The application CV’s URL for this chapter points to nowpublishers.com/article/Details/HPE-0021 — the URL of “The Unintended Consequences of Nation-Making Institutions,” not the OUP chapter. The website has the correct OUP link. Suggested change: Update the title in both documents. Fix the wrong URL in the application CV.


Research — “Rocking Our Priors” attribution misleads; SoundCloud handle reads as anonymous Current: About page links “this podcast” → SoundCloud user-845572280. Both the website and application imply the podcast is by Opalo and Honig. Why it matters: The podcast is hosted by Alice Evans (KCL Senior Lecturer). Linking to “user-845572280” reads like an anonymous SoundCloud account. Suggested change: “I discussed this work on the Rocking Our Priors podcast hosted by Alice Evans, with Ken Opalo and Dan Honig.” Pick a more durable canonical link (Apple Podcasts or Spotify) over the SoundCloud track.


About — first-generation identity claim absent from website Current (website): References “scholars from underrepresented backgrounds” but does not state that Tuğba is herself first-generation. The Other page describes her organising work for first-gen students at MIT but doesn’t say she is one. Why it matters: The application Teaching Statement says: “As a first-generation university student from Turkey who pursued graduate education across Europe and the United States, I am acutely aware of the barriers…” This biographical context strengthens the diversity work and should be visible to a website-only reader. Suggested change: Add to About or Other page: “As a first-generation university student from Turkey, I…”


About — institutional service entirely absent from website Current: No mention. Why it matters: The application CV lists Admissions Chair (Departmental Postgraduate Committee, KCL, 2021–), Departmental Research Committee (KCL, 2022–), and School of Politics and Economics Space Allocation Committee (2024–). For an associate professorship, an Admissions Chair role is exactly the institutional capacity Oxford will care about. Suggested change: Add a short “Institutional service” subsection on the Other page or About.


About — diversity paragraph reads as a sidebar; “Assistant Professor with tenure” is awkward for a UK reader Current: Italicised “In addition to my research, I am deeply interested in diversifying…”; opening uses “Lecturer in Politics & Political Methodology (Assistant Professor with tenure).” Why it matters: The italics and “in addition” hedge make the diversity work read decorative. For a Global South–focused scholar applying to a department that values social policy of the Global South, this commitment is part of professional identity. Separately, the parenthetical “Assistant Professor with tenure” reads as still explaining the title to a US audience for a UK committee. Suggested change: Drop italics and “In addition.” “I am committed to diversifying the representation of the Global South in political economy research and to supporting scholars from underrepresented backgrounds.” Drop the parenthetical or move it to the CV.


Research — Christos Papadimitriou link 403; Salah link likely broken Current: Papadimitriou linked as engineering.columbia.edu/faculty/christos-papadimitriou (403). Salah linked as uu.nl/staff/AAliSalah (likely broken; application uses webspace.science.uu.nl/~salah006/ which works). Suggested change: Fix Papadimitriou to the canonical Columbia URL https://www.engineering.columbia.edu/faculty-staff/directory/christos-papadimitriou; replace Salah with the application’s working URL.


Research — section structure is plain text without visible headings; “Forthcoming” lacks year for AJPS Current: “Publications”, “Working Papers”, “Projects in Progress”, “Policy” appear inline rather than as headings. AJPS entry says “Forthcoming” with no year. Why it matters: Skim-readers miss the AJPS line. “Forthcoming” without a year reads ambiguously between “very recent” and “long-pending.” Suggested change: Mark headings as proper sections. Add expected year to AJPS forthcoming.





Research — replication / data-availability links absent Why it matters: For a Causal and Experimental Methods post, replication links are essentially free credibility. AJPS requires replication archives. Suggested change: Add a “Replication” link next to each empirical paper that has one publicly archived (Dataverse, GitHub).


Research — Policy section ends in 2019 Why it matters: Reads as if public engagement stopped six years ago. Suggested change: Add anything more recent or rename to “Selected Policy Writing.”


Vita — languages, software, training, reviewer activity, meetings organised all missing Why it matters: For a comparative/Global South methods scholar, languages (Turkish, German, Spanish, Ottoman Turkish, Arabic) and software (ArcGIS, Python, R, etc.) are substantively meaningful. Reviewer activity (12 journals including AER, APSR, AJPS, BJPS, CPS) and meetings organised (KCL-UCL-LSE Politics of the Global South 2025–; POLMETH Europe 2023; PEMENA 2022) are standard CV content. Suggested change: Include in the proposed HTML Vita section.


About — closing hobbies sentence reads under-edited Current: “When I’m not working, I enjoy rediscovering the world with my daughter, and if time allows, watching timeless movies, driving, horse riding, reading about Sufism…”; “timeless movies” links to Letterboxd homepage. Suggested change: “Outside of work, I enjoy rediscovering the world with my daughter, watching films, horse riding, reading about Sufism, and spending time in London’s gardens and parks.” Drop or fix the Letterboxd link.


Other — section heading “Other” is generic Suggested change: “Service & Outreach.”


Header / footer — email and GitHub links display as raw URL strings; GitHub repo description is leftover Jekyll boilerplate Suggested change: Set link text to “Email”, “GitHub”, “Google Scholar.” Update the source repo’s GitHub description from “Build a Jekyll blog in minutes…” to something like “Personal academic website (Quarto).”


GIS Tutorial page — links to a GitHub repo with no README Current: The “Tutorial” link goes to GIS-R-Tutorial, which contains only BostonData.zip and an HTML file. Why it matters: For a methods post, this is one of the few public-facing methods-teaching demonstrations and lands on something visibly under-maintained. Suggested change: Add a real README to the repo, or render the tutorial as a Quarto page on the site itself.


Teaching — five Dropbox-hosted MIT TA materials may be unstable Suggested change: Move to GitHub or to the Quarto repo for permanence; verify each Dropbox link still resolves.







The publication record itself is impressive: AJPS and JCR placements, a coherent body of work, prize density visible quickly.
The four substantive research areas (once reframed via the application’s pillar order and language) map onto a real, integrated agenda — no padding.
The site is fast and readable; nothing screams amateurish template.
The first-generation organising work on the Other page is concrete and shows leadership — unusually strong content for a personal site.
Most co-author personal sites are linked and working (Christia, Cansunar, Holland, Sasmaz, Cammett, Nwokolo, Daskalakis) — small touch, signals collegiality.
The site keeps a consistent voice and avoids LinkedIn-ese.
External institutional and publisher links that work: MIT News, KCL, Belfer, Springer (D4R chapters, SCID), OUP, Now Publishers, Foreign Policy, Washington Post, WIDER, GLD, Harvard Data Science, AALIMS, POGS-UCL, J-PAL, Governance Uncovered podcast, Nuffield, MIT polisci.

title: Website Review — Tuğba Bozçağa (https://tugbabozcaga.github.io/)
text:

The “Paper” link under “Putting Property Rights in Context” (Mozambique) resolves to abstract_id=5397681 — “The Social Bureaucrat.” Why it matters: The flagship AJPS publication and the most DSPI-legible working paper both open onto each other. After the swap, open both links to confirm they resolve to the right papers before publishing.


Research — eight links route to empty Wix template pages Current: Links to tugbabozcaga.com/awardcitation1, forbearancedilution (used twice — once on the Springer chapter, once on the Holland/SCID paper), education-localcouncils, gender-meritocracy, education-dilemma, plus the Teaching page syllabus links syllabus-7aaom041 and syllabus7aaom230. All resolve to the same Wix template — header reading “Tuğba Bozçağa / Assistant Professor in Politics & Political Methodology, King’s College London / tugba.bozcaga@kcl.ac.uk” — with no paper, appendix, citation, or syllabus underneath. Worse, the Wix template still describes her as “Assistant Professor” with a stale bozcaga@mit.edu contact, contradicting the main site. Why it matters: These links promise specific content (drafts, appendices, the citation for an APSA award, KCL syllabi) and deliver nothing. To a careful reader this looks worse than a 404 — it suggests the site is built on dead stubs. The application CV also links to two of these stubs (education-localcouncils, education-dilemma), so a committee member clicking from the application document lands on the same empty pages. Suggested change: Replace each with a working link (direct PDF, SSRN, Dataverse, institutional URL) or remove until the underlying file exists. Coordinate the same fix in the application CV.


All pages — Google Scholar link is a placeholder Current: https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=YOUR_ID in the header of all six pages. Why it matters: Most visible “unfinished site” signal on the entire site. The real profile exists. Suggested change: Replace with https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=rkJvZccAAAAJ&hl=en.


Research — “Imams and Patrons” listed as “Forthcoming” but published in JCR (Sept 2025) Current (both website and application): “Forthcoming in Journal of Conflict Resolution”; “Paper” link → SSRN abstract_id=5397663. Why it matters: The paper has been published online in JCR since September 2025 (DOI 10.1177/00220027251374830). Listing it as forthcoming understates the record. The SSRN page at 5397663 returns 403 to outside fetches; v1 was wrong to claim the ID is invalid, but the right move regardless is to point readers at the published version, not SSRN. Suggested change: Update both website and application CV to: “‘Imams and Patrons: Service Provision by Islamist Non-State Actors’ (with Fotini Christia). Journal of Conflict Resolution, 2025.” Replace the SSRN link with the published Sage URL: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00220027251374830.


Research — Mozambique paper missing fourth co-author (Pita Barros) Current: Listed on the website as “with Robin Harding and Arinze Nwokolo.” Why it matters: The application Research Statement lists “Robin Harding (Oxford), Arinze Nwokolo (Lagos Business School), and Henrique Pita Barros (ISEG Lisbon).” The website is missing one co-author of a paper described as “about to be submitted to APSR.” Authorship omissions are taken seriously. Suggested change: Add Pita Barros to the website entry. Match the application’s authorship list exactly.


Research — three MPSA award links and three more dead/broken links Current (About page): mpsanet.org/professional-resources/awards/2022-award-recipients/ is used three times for Pi Sigma Alpha, Kenneth Meier, and Best Paper by an Emerging Scholar — all 404. Research page: Robin Harding linked as robingharding.org (extra “g,” broken); Rabia Kutlu linked as rabiakutlu.com (dead domain, used twice); Turkish Policy Quarterly paper links to turkishpolicy.com (now a “domain for sale” page). Why it matters: Three broken links in the most-read paragraph of the About page; broken co-author links to two scholars (Harding is at Oxford DPIR — the appointing department); her earliest publication unreachable. The application CV uses correct URLs for Harding and Kutlu’s Stanford page; only the website has the broken versions. Suggested change: Update MPSA links to mpsanet.org/professional-resources/awards/award-recipient-archive/. Fix Harding to https://robinharding.org/ and Kutlu to https://politicalscience.stanford.edu/people/rabia-kutlu-karasu. For TPQ, find an archived copy (Wayback, ResearchGate) or remove the link and keep the citation.


Other — five MIT/first-gen links dead or 404; APSA committee URL inconsistent with About page Current: (a) oge.mit.edu/finances/graduate-student-life-grants/ → 404; (b) firstgen.mit.edu/ and (c) firstgen.mit.edu/resources → dead domain (MIT FGP moved to advising.mit.edu/fli/); (d) oge.mit.edu/community-diversity/dei-committee/ → 404; (e) APSA First-Gen Committee URL (/RESOURCES/For-Faculty/...) errors out, while the About page uses a different working URL. Why it matters: Five out of nine substantive links on a page that anchors her first-gen organising work are broken; the same APSA committee gets two different (one broken, one working) URLs across the site. Suggested change: Replace MIT FGP links with https://advising.mit.edu/fli/; remove or replace the dead OGE links; use the working APSA committee URL from the About page consistently.


About — research framing diverges from application Research Statement Current (website): “My research focuses on the political economy of development, particularly public service provision and social welfare.” Why it matters: The application opens with stronger DSPI-legible framing — “political economy of development, with an emphasis on service provision and social welfare” — gives a different pillar order, and identifies colonial extraction and disaster resilience as her forward research agenda. None of this strategic framing is on the website. A committee reading both will read the website as a stale, pre-strategic version of the candidate. Suggested change: Port the application Research Statement opening directly to the About page. Match the application’s pillar order: (1) state capacity / service delivery; (2) colonial extraction; (3) refugee mobility & climate vulnerability; (4) disaster resilience.


About — methods sentence undersells for a CASSM-targeted post Current (website): “I study these issues … through quasi-experimental statistical designs and novel data sources, often supplemented by fieldwork and archival research.” Why it matters: The post is “Causal and Experimental Methods in Politics and Social Policy.” The application names methods specifically; the website doesn’t. Suggested change (adapted, not ported verbatim): “Methodologically, I use causal and quasi-experimental designs — including spatial regression discontinuity, difference-in-differences, event-study, panel, and spatial econometric approaches — combined with fieldwork, archival research, and novel data sources such as satellite imagery, administrative data, and mobile-phone records.”


Research — Oxford DPIR Visiting Scholar (2024) entirely missing Current (application CV): “2024 University of Oxford. Visiting Scholar, Department of Politics and IR.” Why it matters: Of all positions on the CV, this one is the strongest possible signal for this specific committee — she has held a visiting position in the appointing department. Invisible on the website. Suggested change: Add to About page. Combine with Nuffield, phrased as past since the application CV gives 2024 with no end-date marker: “In 2024, I was a Visiting Scholar at Oxford’s Department of Politics and International Relations, and I am an Associate Member of Nuffield College, Oxford.”


Research — five working papers and two in-progress projects are title-only Current (website): “Employment Type and Refugees’ Climate Vulnerability…”, “Regulatory Failures in Disaster-Prone Times…”, “Scarcity and Discrimination in Local Public Services…”, “Urban Bias in Rural Governance…” — titles only. No links, abstracts, or one-line descriptions. Why it matters: These are the most DSPI-legible projects on the entire site. Title-only listings make them invisible. The application has detailed paragraphs on the climate vulnerability paper (CORINE land cover, mobile CDRs, temperature/precipitation) and the wildfire paper (privatisation, electoral records, NASA Global Fire Atlas, difference-in-differences). The application also reveals: “When Incumbent Mayors…” is “About to be submitted to American Journal of Political Science” and the Mozambique paper is “About to be submitted to American Political Science Review” — submission status absent from website. Suggested change: Port one-or-two-sentence descriptions from the Research Statement. Add submission status where the application provides it.


Vita — page is essentially empty AND the linked CV PDF is older than the application CV Current: The Vita page contains only a download link. The website’s cv.pdf is “Last updated August 2025.” The application CV is “Last updated April 2026.” Why it matters: Two different CV documents are circulating. A reader following the website link gets an older version than the one accompanying the application — and the August 2025 version contains “Phi Bheta Kappa Award” (typo), “Imams and Businessmen” (outdated paper title), and the now-stale “forthcoming” status for Imams and Patrons. References will likely receive the April 2026 version; the committee, comparing, will see drift. Suggested change: (a) Replace cv.pdf with the corrected April 2026 application CV (after fixing Pi Sigma Alpha and the propagated URL errors); (b) add a short HTML version of key CV sections (Education, Positions, Selected Awards, Recent Talks, Service) to the Vita page; (c) include a “Last updated” date.


Application document — MPSA award name appears five different ways across her own materials Current: Application Research Statement: “MPSA Phi Beta Kappa Award.” Application CV Publications section: “Phi Beta Kappa Award, MPSA.” Application CV Awards section: “MPSA Phi Sigma Alpha Award.” Website About: “Pi Sigma Alpha Award” (correct). Website CV PDF: “Phi Bheta Kappa Award” (typo of the wrong honor society). Why it matters: The correct MPSA prize is Pi Sigma Alpha. “Phi Beta Kappa” is a different, unrelated honor society — the application document has named the wrong organisation in two of three places. Anyone on the committee who knows MPSA will catch this. Five versions of the same award name across the candidate’s documents is not survivable. Suggested change: Standardise on “MPSA Pi Sigma Alpha Award (Best Paper Presented at the Annual Conference)” across application Research Statement, both CV sections, website About page, and website CV PDF.


Teaching — doctoral and dissertation supervision claim missing entirely from website Current: No mention of doctoral supervision on the website Teaching page. Why it matters: The application Teaching Statement says she supervises ~12 BA/MA dissertations per year and co-supervises four doctoral students. For a permanent post that involves doctoral training, evidence of supervision capacity should be findable. Suggested change (softer than the bureaucratic application phrasing): Add to the Teaching page: “I supervise undergraduate, master’s, and doctoral research projects in comparative political economy, political methodology, public service delivery, migration, and social welfare.” (The exact “all four passed upgrades without extension” detail belongs in the Teaching Statement, not the public site.)


About / Research — AALIMS title and APSA PE role contradict the application CV Current (website): “Junior Fellow at AALIMS”; “member of APSA’s Political Economy Section Committee.” Why it matters: The application CV (April 2026, Tuğba’s own canonical document) says “Faculty Fellow, AALIMS, 2021–” and “Council Member of the APSA Political Economy Section, 2024–.” Faculty Fellow is more senior than Junior Fellow at AALIMS, and Council Member is a more specific role than generic Section Committee member. The website is downgrading her own current titles. Suggested change: Update the website to match the application: “Faculty Fellow at AALIMS”; “Council Member of the APSA Political Economy Section.” No further verification needed — the application CV is the source.


Research — wildfire paper has three different titles across application, website, and website CV PDF Current: Application Research Statement and CV: “Privatization without Regulation: The Political Economy of Electricity Infrastructure and Wildfires.” Website Research page: “Regulatory Failures in Disaster-Prone Times: How Electricity Privatization Shapes Wildfire Outcomes.” Website CV PDF: “Regulatory Failures in Disaster-Prone Areas…”. Why it matters: Three titles for the same paper across documents the committee will read together. Inconsistency reads as carelessness even if it reflects an honest revision history. Suggested change: Standardise on the application’s “Privatization without Regulation…” version (cleanest, most CASSM-legible) across all three documents.





Research — Recent Talks section absent from website; Oxford DPIR and DSPI talks invisible Current: No talks/presentations section. Why it matters: The application CV lists 2025 talks at Oxford DPIR Comparative Politics Seminar Series and 2022 talks at Oxford DSPI Seminar Series and Oxford DPIR Seminar Series — i.e. talks to both halves of the appointing committee. “She’s already presented in our department” is one of the strongest possible signals; currently invisible to anyone without the CV PDF open. Suggested change: Add a “Recent Talks” subsection at the bottom of Research (or on Vita), listing 2024–2026 talks with the Oxford ones leading. Port the entire “Recent Talks & Presentations” section from the application CV.


About — bio omits 2024 KCL Performance Recognition Award Current: No mention; prize list ends with 2022 MPSA awards. Why it matters: The application CV’s most recent award is 2024. The website makes the recognition trail look three years old. Suggested change: Add to the About prize list, leading because most recent.


About — current research and forward-looking signal absent Current: Bio ends on dissertation/early-postdoc-era prizes. Why it matters: Reads backwards-looking. The application identifies a forward agenda (colonial extraction, disaster resilience), submitted-to-AJPS and submitted-to-APSR papers, MZES workshop, and 2024 KCL recognition. Suggested change: Add 1–2 forward-looking sentences. Whether to name the ERC/UKRI/Wellcome grant pipeline publicly is Tuğba’s call — naming specific funders before submission is more aggressive than many candidates do publicly. A safer version: “My current research extends this work into the long-run consequences of colonial extraction and the political economy of regulation, infrastructure, and disaster resilience.” (If she wants the funder names public, append: “…and forms the basis of grant applications I am currently preparing.”)


About — Nuffield title and KCL title need verification and standardisation Current: Website says “Associate Faculty Member at Nuffield.” Application CV says “Associate Member, Nuffield College.” Research/Teaching Statement headers say “Lecturer in Politics (Political Methodology)”; website + application CV say “Lecturer in Politics & Political Methodology”; KCL’s main faculty page may use yet another version. Why it matters: The committee will read statements + website + CV together. Two title formats for the same role look inattentive. Suggested change: Verify Nuffield’s actual designation — “Associate Member” is the application’s version and is a real Nuffield category. For KCL, verify against the KCL faculty page and standardise across all four documents.


Other — Development Analytics description undersells DSPI relevance Current: “Development Analytics is an Oxford-based research institute that conducts evidence-based research on social programs and policy development.” Why it matters: Development Analytics is dual-located (UK Companies House registers it at 9 Marlborough Court, Oxford OX2 0QT; the institute’s contact page also lists Istanbul). Geography isn’t the issue — but the substantive areas (poverty, education, health, social protection, distributional impact of social policies) are highly DSPI-relevant and the description currently doesn’t surface them. Suggested change: “Development Analytics is a research centre and advisory working on poverty, education, health, social protection, humanitarian aid, and the distributional impact of social policies. I am a Research Associate.”


Teaching — page jumps from header to module list with no framing; no eval scores or enrolment-expansion fact Current: No teaching paragraph; modules listed as codes only; three modules have a stray ::: Quarto artefact (“PE of Development in Muslim Societies:::”, etc.). Why it matters: For a half-DSPI post, a 3–4 sentence intro signalling teaching range matters. The application Teaching Statement notes that Quantitative Research Methods received “some of the highest student assessment scores,” led to enrolment expansion, and seeded a similar undergraduate module. The website CV PDF lists evaluations of 4.7/5 (Quant Methods), 4.4/5 (PE of Development in Muslim Societies), 4.2/5 (Comparative Politics) — none on the public Teaching page. Suggested change: Fix the ::: artefacts. Add a brief intro paragraph: “My teaching spans quantitative methods, research design, comparative politics, and the political economy of development, with an emphasis on helping students apply rigorous empirical tools to questions of governance, inequality, public service delivery, migration, and social welfare.” Add level/audience and a 1-sentence content gloss per module. Surface the enrolment-expansion fact for Quant Methods.


Teaching — MZES Mannheim 2026 workshop and KCL Methods Centre roundtables absent Current: Neither mentioned. Why it matters: The application says she will deliver the Advanced Geospatial Analysis workshop at the MZES Summer School for Women in Political Methodology (May 2026) — a forward-looking, prestigious methods signal during the appointment process. Also chaired KCL Social Sciences Methods Centre PhD roundtables. Suggested change: Add both to the Teaching page (or the proposed HTML Vita) once dates and roles are confirmed.


Research — Springer chapter title and online-appendix link need correction (but the URL _12 is correct) Current: The entry is titled “Assessing Syrian Refugee Integration Using Call Detail Records from Turkey.” The Springer link link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-12554-7_12 opens the right chapter (verified). The “Online Appendix” link points to the unrelated forbearancedilution Wix stub. Why it matters: The published Springer title is “Syrian Refugee Integration in Turkey: Evidence from Call Detail Records.” The website and application CV both still use the working-paper title. The appendix link promises supplementary material but lands on an empty page. Suggested change: Update the title in both website and application CV to the published version. Keep the Springer _12 link as-is — it works. Remove or replace the “Online Appendix” link.


Research — OUP chapter title differs from published; application CV uses the wrong URL Current: Both documents use “Combining Mobile Data and Satellite Imaging for Human Mobility.” The OUP-published title is “Combining Mobile Call Data and Satellite Imaging for Human Mobility.” The application CV’s URL for this chapter points to nowpublishers.com/article/Details/HPE-0021 — the URL of “The Unintended Consequences of Nation-Making Institutions,” not the OUP chapter. The website has the correct OUP link. Suggested change: Update the title in both documents. Fix the wrong URL in the application CV.


Research — “Rocking Our Priors” attribution misleads; SoundCloud handle reads as anonymous Current: About page links “this podcast” → SoundCloud user-845572280. Both the website and application imply the podcast is by Opalo and Honig. Why it matters: The podcast is hosted by Alice Evans (KCL Senior Lecturer). Linking to “user-845572280” reads like an anonymous SoundCloud account. Suggested change: “I discussed this work on the Rocking Our Priors podcast hosted by Alice Evans, with Ken Opalo and Dan Honig.” Pick a more durable canonical link (Apple Podcasts or Spotify) over the SoundCloud track.


About — first-generation identity claim absent from website Current (website): References “scholars from underrepresented backgrounds” but does not state that Tuğba is herself first-generation. The Other page describes her organising work for first-gen students at MIT but doesn’t say she is one. Why it matters: The application Teaching Statement says: “As a first-generation university student from Turkey who pursued graduate education across Europe and the United States, I am acutely aware of the barriers…” This biographical context strengthens the diversity work and should be visible to a website-only reader. Suggested change: Add to About or Other page: “As a first-generation university student from Turkey, I…”


About — institutional service entirely absent from website Current: No mention. Why it matters: The application CV lists Admissions Chair (Departmental Postgraduate Committee, KCL, 2021–), Departmental Research Committee (KCL, 2022–), and School of Politics and Economics Space Allocation Committee (2024–). For an associate professorship, an Admissions Chair role is exactly the institutional capacity Oxford will care about. Suggested change: Add a short “Institutional service” subsection on the Other page or About.


About — diversity paragraph reads as a sidebar; “Assistant Professor with tenure” is awkward for a UK reader Current: Italicised “In addition to my research, I am deeply interested in diversifying…”; opening uses “Lecturer in Politics & Political Methodology (Assistant Professor with tenure).” Why it matters: The italics and “in addition” hedge make the diversity work read decorative. For a Global South–focused scholar applying to a department that values social policy of the Global South, this commitment is part of professional identity. Separately, the parenthetical “Assistant Professor with tenure” reads as still explaining the title to a US audience for a UK committee. Suggested change: Drop italics and “In addition.” “I am committed to diversifying the representation of the Global South in political economy research and to supporting scholars from underrepresented backgrounds.” Drop the parenthetical or move it to the CV.


Research — Christos Papadimitriou link 403; Salah link likely broken Current: Papadimitriou linked as engineering.columbia.edu/faculty/christos-papadimitriou (403). Salah linked as uu.nl/staff/AAliSalah (likely broken; application uses webspace.science.uu.nl/~salah006/ which works). Suggested change: Fix Papadimitriou to the canonical Columbia URL https://www.engineering.columbia.edu/faculty-staff/directory/christos-papadimitriou; replace Salah with the application’s working URL.


Research — section structure is plain text without visible headings; “Forthcoming” lacks year for AJPS Current: “Publications”, “Working Papers”, “Projects in Progress”, “Policy” appear inline rather than as headings. AJPS entry says “Forthcoming” with no year. Why it matters: Skim-readers miss the AJPS line. “Forthcoming” without a year reads ambiguously between “very recent” and “long-pending.” Suggested change: Mark headings as proper sections. Add expected year to AJPS forthcoming.





Research — replication / data-availability links absent Why it matters: For a Causal and Experimental Methods post, replication links are essentially free credibility. AJPS requires replication archives. Suggested change: Add a “Replication” link next to each empirical paper that has one publicly archived (Dataverse, GitHub).


Research — Policy section ends in 2019 Why it matters: Reads as if public engagement stopped six years ago. Suggested change: Add anything more recent or rename to “Selected Policy Writing.”


Vita — languages, software, training, reviewer activity, meetings organised all missing Why it matters: For a comparative/Global South methods scholar, languages (Turkish, German, Spanish, Ottoman Turkish, Arabic) and software (ArcGIS, Python, R, etc.) are substantively meaningful. Reviewer activity (12 journals including AER, APSR, AJPS, BJPS, CPS) and meetings organised (KCL-UCL-LSE Politics of the Global South 2025–; POLMETH Europe 2023; PEMENA 2022) are standard CV content. Suggested change: Include in the proposed HTML Vita section.


About — closing hobbies sentence reads under-edited Current: “When I’m not working, I enjoy rediscovering the world with my daughter, and if time allows, watching timeless movies, driving, horse riding, reading about Sufism…”; “timeless movies” links to Letterboxd homepage. Suggested change: “Outside of work, I enjoy rediscovering the world with my daughter, watching films, horse riding, reading about Sufism, and spending time in London’s gardens and parks.” Drop or fix the Letterboxd link.


Other — section heading “Other” is generic Suggested change: “Service & Outreach.”


Header / footer — email and GitHub links display as raw URL strings; GitHub repo description is leftover Jekyll boilerplate Suggested change: Set link text to “Email”, “GitHub”, “Google Scholar.” Update the source repo’s GitHub description from “Build a Jekyll blog in minutes…” to something like “Personal academic website (Quarto).”


GIS Tutorial page — links to a GitHub repo with no README Current: The “Tutorial” link goes to GIS-R-Tutorial, which contains only BostonData.zip and an HTML file. Why it matters: For a methods post, this is one of the few public-facing methods-teaching demonstrations and lands on something visibly under-maintained. Suggested change: Add a real README to the repo, or render the tutorial as a Quarto page on the site itself.


Teaching — five Dropbox-hosted MIT TA materials may be unstable Suggested change: Move to GitHub or to the Quarto repo for permanence; verify each Dropbox link still resolves.

title: Website Review — Tuğba Bozçağa (https://tugbabozcaga.github.io/)
text:
The publication record itself is impressive: AJPS and JCR placements, a coherent body of work, prize density visible quickly.
The four substantive research areas (once reframed via the application’s pillar order and language) map onto a real, integrated agenda — no padding.
The site is fast and readable; nothing screams amateurish template.
The first-generation organising work on the Other page is concrete and shows leadership — unusually strong content for a personal site.
Most co-author personal sites are linked and working (Christia, Cansunar, Holland, Sasmaz, Cammett, Nwokolo, Daskalakis) — small touch, signals collegiality.
The site keeps a consistent voice and avoids LinkedIn-ese.
External institutional and publisher links that work: MIT News, KCL, Belfer, Springer (D4R chapters, SCID), OUP, Now Publishers, Foreign Policy, Washington Post, WIDER, GLD, Harvard Data Science, AALIMS, POGS-UCL, J-PAL, Governance Uncovered podcast, Nuffield, MIT polisci.

MIT First-Gen Initiative for Graduate Students

In March 2019, I organized a kickoff event to introduce a new first-generation network for graduate students at MIT. The dinner was sponsored by the Office of Graduate Education through a Graduate Student Life Grant, with help from the First-Generation and Low-Income Program. The invitation was for graduate students at MIT (Post-doc, PhD, or MA) whose parent(s) had not received a college degree and/or who came from low-income households.
MIT’s existing first-gen programming targets undergraduate students and has successfully supported them. Yet, in many cases, the support first-generation students need becomes even greater at the graduate level. This event, therefore, aimed to launch a similar initiative for graduate students and provided an opportunity for them to meet each other and brainstorm how best to support future first-generation graduate students.
In 2019–2020, I served as the inaugural constituency representative of first-generation students at MIT’s Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Committee.

APSA Committee on the Status of First-Generation Scholars

I serve as a member of the APSA Committee on the Status of First-Generation Scholars. You can find information about the committee and its grant announcements on this page.

Development Analytics, Research Associate

Development Analytics is a research centre and advisory working on poverty, education, health, social protection, humanitarian aid, and the distributional impact of social policies. I am a Research Associate.

title: Geospatial Analysis in R
text:
I designed this tutorial originally for the MIT Political Science Methods Workshop series for graduate students and faculty members. It teaches how to make maps and geospatial calculations in R.
You will learn:

What are the main components of spatial data
How we can combine spatial data with other data sources
How we can create and manipulate maps
Spatial regression techniques

This tutorial is good for students with some familiarity with R, but does not require previous knowledge of geospatial analysis.

title: Tuğba Bozçağa
text:
I am a Lecturer in Politics & Political Methodology (Assistant Professor with tenure) at King’s College London. Previously, I was a Postdoctoral Fellow at Harvard Kennedy School’s Middle East Initiative. I completed my PhD in September 2020 in the Department of Political Science at Massachusetts Institute of Technology. I am also an Associate Member of Nuffield College at the University of Oxford. In 2024, I was a Visiting Scholar at Oxford’s Department of Politics and International Relations.
My research focuses on the political economy of development, particularly public service provision and social welfare. My previous and ongoing projects concentrate on four areas: (1) the relationship between state capacity, accountability, and public goods provision, with particular attention to spatial factors and ethno-religious heterogeneity; (2) spatial integration and climate resilience of refugee populations; (3) disaster resilience in rural and urban governance; and (4) the long-term influence of colonial interventions on development outcomes. I study these issues in Global South contexts through quasi-experimental statistical designs and novel data sources, often supplemented by fieldwork and archival research.
My papers have been published or are forthcoming in journals such as the American Journal of Political Science, Journal of Conflict Resolution, and Studies in Comparative International Development. My work has received several prizes, including the American Political Science Association’s (APSA) Mancur Olson Best Dissertation Prize (Honorable Mention) for Best Dissertation in Political Economy, McGillivray Award for Best Paper in Political Economy (Honorable Mention), Weber Best Conference Paper Award for Best Paper in Religion and Politics, Best Comparative Policy Paper Award, Best Paper Award in MENA Politics, and the Midwest Political Science Association’s Pi Sigma Alpha Award for Best Paper, Kenneth Meier Award for Best Paper in Public Administration or Public Policy, and Best Paper by an Emerging Scholar Award. My research has been supported by the Harvard Data Science Initiative, Program on Governance and Local Development, and MIT Center for International Studies.
In addition to my research, I am deeply interested in diversifying the representation of underrepresented regions, particularly Global South, in political economy research, as well as enhancing the inclusion of scholars from underrepresented backgrounds in our discipline. I also serve as a Council Member of APSA’s Political Economy Section and Committee on the Status of First-Generation Higher Education Scholars in the Profession. I am a Faculty Fellow at the Association for Analytic Learning about Islam and Muslim Societies (AALIMS). I serve on the organizing committee of the Politics of the Global South (POGS) working group.
You can find a discussion about my research in this podcast and this news article. When I’m not working, I enjoy rediscovering the world with my daughter, and if time allows, watching films, driving, horse riding, reading about Sufism, and spending quiet times in London’s beautiful gardens and parks.

title: Research Statement
text:
Tuğba Bozçağa Lecturer in Politics (Political Methodology), King’s College London tugbabozcaga.github.io | tugba.bozcaga@kcl.ac.uk
My research examines the political economy of development, with an emphasis on service provision and social welfare. My work spans four interconnected areas: (1) state capacity and accountability in public service delivery, with particular attention to ethno-religious heterogeneity and spatial dynamics; (2) the long-term developmental consequences of extractive colonial institutions; (3) the spatial mobility, integration, and climate vulnerability of refugee populations; and (4) the political economy of disasters, especially vulnerability to natural hazards and climate change across urban and rural governance settings. The first pillar is grounded in published and forthcoming work, while the third extends research on refugee welfare to address climate vulnerability. My work on the political economy of disaster resilience, together with research on colonial extraction and its developmental consequences, forms my forward research agenda. These strands underpin grant applications currently in preparation for the European Research Council, the UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship, and the Wellcome Trust.
I study these policy-relevant questions by combining quasi-experimental designs with novel data sources. My commitment to studying causally identified questions in Global South contexts operates under conditions where administrative data are often limited and randomized experimentation is frequently infeasible due to political constraints, instability, or weak state capacity. My focus on quasi-experimental designs and novel data sources reflects a broader commitment to studying understudied, institutionally constrained, and often autocratic or weak-state contexts. Across projects, I employ spatial regression discontinuity designs, difference-in-differences, event studies, panel methods, and spatial econometric techniques. To address data limitations, I invest in innovative measurement strategies, including remote sensing, deep learning applied to satellite imagery, network measures derived from mobile call detail records, automated web scraping, and the digitization of archival and ethnographic sources.


My paper, “The Social Bureaucrat: How Social Proximity among Bureaucrats Affects Local Governance” (forthcoming, American Journal of Political Science), develops a theory of bureaucratic efficiency that complements accountability-based explanations of service delivery with a capacity-based mechanism: efficiency increases with social proximity among bureaucrats, as informal ties reduce the coordination and transaction costs of public service provision. I test this argument using a spatial regression discontinuity design and novel data on rural water infrastructure across more than 35,000 villages in Turkey, combined with network measures constructed from antenna-level mobile call detail records and an original dataset mapping the ethno-religious distribution of villages. The paper has received the APSA Best Comparative Policy Paper Award, the MPSA Phi Beta Kappa Award, the MPSA Kenneth Meier Award for Best Paper in Public Policy and Administration, and the MPSA Best Paper by an Emerging Scholar Award, among others.
A companion paper with Fotini Christia (MIT), “Imams and Patrons: Service Provision by Islamist Non-State Actors” (forthcoming, Journal of Conflict Resolution), analyzes spatial and temporal variation in the service networks of an Islamist non-state actor across Turkey’s 970 districts, showing that non-state welfare provision depends critically on the movement’s ability to mobilize local economic elites rather than on strategic political calculation alone. A third paper, “Members of the Same Club?: Subnational Variations in Electoral Returns to Public Goods” (APSA McGillivray Honorable Mention), uses a generalized difference-in-differences design to show that electoral returns to local public goods increase with their perceived excludability, except where identity-based cleavages attenuate this relationship.
Extending this pillar to the enforcement dimension of state capacity, my co-authored paper with Alisha Holland (Harvard), “Enforcement Process Tracing: Forbearance and Dilution in Urban Colombia and Turkey” (Studies in Comparative International Development), shows that enforcement decisions regarding informal housing and businesses vary systematically over electoral cycles. Alongside this research, I was invited to author “Municipal Government” in Oxford Bibliographies in Urban Studies (Oxford University Press, 2025), which synthesizes the comparative literature on local government.



My second research pillar examines the long-term impact of extractive colonial interventions on political institutions, public service provision, and human development in sub-Saharan Africa. With Robin Harding (Oxford), Arinze Nwokolo (Lagos Business School), and Henrique Pita Barros (ISEG Lisbon), I am developing a coordinated set of projects examining this question. Our first paper, “Putting Property Rights in Context: Colonial Cotton Concessions, Customary Land Tenure, and Development in Mozambique,” draws on archival maps of colonial concession boundaries and implements a spatial regression discontinuity design to assess the long-run consequences of coercive agricultural production in Mozambique. Contrary to canonical theories in institutional economics associated with Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson, we find that areas subjected to extractive colonial rule exhibit worse long-run education- and health-related outcomes and weaker public service infrastructure, despite higher rates of private land and home ownership today: by eroding customary land authorities, extractive institutions weakened local collective action and diminished the resources available for communal service provision. Building on this work, my co-authors and I are preparing a large-scale Wellcome Trust and ERC application examining the long-term impact of extractive colonial interventions on political institutions, public service provision, and human development in sub-Saharan Africa. We are extending this framework to additional cases in sub-Saharan Africa to examine the impact of different types of extractive interventions on current political institutions, policy implementation, and development outcomes.



This pillar investigates how displaced populations integrate into host societies, including spatial mobility, segregation, and exposure to environmental risk, using panel designs. Two book chapters, in Guide to Mobile Data Analytics in Refugee Scenarios (Springer, 2019) and Data Science for Migration and Mobility (Oxford University Press, 2022), draw on geocoded and time-stamped mobile call detail records from more than 400,000 Syrian refugees and 1 million Turkish citizens to develop measures of spatial mobility and integration. They also show that combining mobile data with satellite imagery, and explicitly accounting for spatial distance, improves the measurement of refugees’ mobility and settlement patterns relative to conventional indicators aggregated at administrative levels.
A current working paper, “Employment Type and Refugees’ Climate Vulnerability: Evidence from Geocoded Mobility Patterns during Seasonal Agricultural Employment,” integrates geocoded mobile call detail records with high-resolution data on temperature extremes and precipitation, as well as processed geospatial land cover data (e.g., CORINE) to identify patterns of seasonal agricultural employment. It examines whether refugees engaged in seasonal work are disproportionately exposed to climate hazards relative to natives, with direct implications for refugee welfare and social protection policies in host countries across the Mediterranean and beyond.



This stream represents a newly emerging research agenda that I am actively developing alongside the colonial-extraction pillar described above, and it constitutes one of the two core pillars underlying my ERC and UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship applications. It examines the political economy of disaster resilience, focusing on how privatized service delivery and political competition shape local vulnerability to natural disasters through the weak regulatory enforcement of private infrastructure and service providers. I measure resilience through variation in damage from natural disasters such as wildfires, floods, and earthquakes, drawing on cases severely affected by recent events, including Spain, Pakistan, Turkey, and California.
To construct comparable measures of damage where processed geospatial data are unavailable, I use deep-learning approaches applied to remote sensing and satellite imagery, an approach that is particularly valuable in Global South contexts where political and administrative constraints limit access to official data. My first working paper in this agenda, “Privatization without Regulation: The Political Economy of Electricity Infrastructure and Wildfires,” shows that the privatisation of electricity services leads to deteriorating infrastructure quality and higher wildfire incidence under weak regulatory enforcement. It also examines how this relationship varies across political contexts, testing whether electoral districts represented by opposition politicians are more resilient than their counterparts despite privatisation. I evaluate this argument using a difference-in-differences design that combines electricity outage data, electoral records, the NASA Global Fire Atlas, and geocoded wildfire incidents across Turkey.

title: Research Statement
text:
Teaching Experience
My research and training equip me to teach across undergraduate and graduate programmes at DSPI and DPIR. On the methods side, I would contribute teaching in causal inference, statistics, econometrics, experimental methods, impact evaluation, and data science in R, and develop new offerings in advanced geospatial analysis and machine learning for policy applications. On the substantive side, I would offer and design courses on comparative politics, the political economy of development, comparative public policy, bureaucracy and the state, urban and local politics, the politics of disaster resilience, migration and displacement, and the politics of development in the Middle East.
At King’s, I have designed and convened three modules. My MA-level Quantitative Research Methods module pairs lectures on causal identification and econometrics with weekly hands-on R lab sessions and has received some of the highest student assessment scores. Following its success, the department expanded enrolment and introduced a similar undergraduate-level course into the core BA curriculum. My MA-level Political Economy of Development in Muslim Societies pairs comparative arguments with empirical applications from Muslim-majority contexts. I have also co-convened the BA core module Introduction to Politics (with over 100 students annually). I currently supervise approximately twelve BA and MA dissertations per year and co-supervise four doctoral students; all four have passed their upgrades without extension and are on track to complete on time.
I served as chair of quantitative methods roundtables for PhD students at the King’s School of Social Sciences and Public Policy Methods Centre. In May 2026, I will deliver the Advanced Geospatial Analysis workshop at the MZES Summer School for Women in Political Methodology at the University of Mannheim, and I have organised major methods events, including POLMETH Europe (2023).
My prior teaching includes graduate-level courses at MIT (Quantitative Methodology I: Regression (instructor: Daniel Hidalgo) and Machine Learning and Data Science in Politics (instructor: In Song Kim)), workshops in LaTeX, GitHub, and geospatial analysis at MIT’s Political Methodology Lab, and a teaching assistantship in J-PAL’s Executive Education course in causal inference for government and NGO practitioners.

title: Research Statement
text:
Teaching Philosophy
Classroom inclusiveness. The graduate cohorts at DSPI and DPIR draw students from across the world and from fields as varied as computer science, economics, law, and public administration, and my experience teaching similarly heterogeneous cohorts has shaped how I design my modules. As a first-generation university student from Turkey who pursued graduate education across Europe and the United States, I am acutely aware of the barriers that students from varied starting points may face. In practice, I use anonymous online forums where reluctant students can raise questions, foster an inclusive discussion environment by emphasising that each student brings distinctive knowledge to the classroom, and share annotated tutorials and datasets through GitHub.
Mentorship. My approach to advising is to begin with students’ own research questions and help them assess the trade-offs between topics, methods, and data sources, rather than directing them toward a pre-set approach. I am ready to take on primary doctoral supervision at Oxford and am particularly committed to supporting students from underrepresented backgrounds, as reflected in my service on the APSA Committee on the Status of First Generation Scholars and the APSA Political Economy Section, as well as my fellowship with the Association for Analytic Learning about Islam and Muslim Societies.
Making technical material accessible. Teaching causal inference, data science, and quantitative methods to students with varied technical backgrounds requires care in design and delivery. I prioritise intuitive explanations and worked examples before introducing formal notation, and pair each methods lecture with a hands-on R lab session, consistently identified as the most valuable feature in student feedback. I prepare supplementary materials, tutorials, and annotated code and share them on GitHub and RPubs so they remain accessible after formal training ends.
